stem: A reading group summarizes Kasch's foundational claim as: 'projection and undercraft are just two independent skills, so a performer's projection score tells you nothing at all about their undercraft.' What is the most important thing this summary gets wrong?

options.text: Projection and undercraft are not merely unrelated but negatively associated, so a strong projection score does predict something specific: on average, weaker undercraft skill, not an absence of any pattern.
Projection and undercraft are really one underlying stage-skill quality, so a performer who commands an audience's attention is also likely to be strong at holding a scene together backstage.
options.provenance: misreads 'Projection is, by definition, what the audience is watching' as implying stage skill is one unified quality

options.text: Projection and undercraft scores are simply uncorrelated, so a strong projector is exactly as likely to have strong undercraft as weak, with no direction to the relationship either way.
options.provenance: misreads 'not two ends of one scale' as meaning the two axes are merely unrelated rather than pulling against each other

options.text: Training projection and training undercraft are independent processes, so a performer who spent years training projection has not thereby lost any capacity for undercraft skill.
options.provenance: misreads 'separately acquired, separately trained' as a claim of independence, missing that pushing projection actively degrades undercraft capacity

explanation: Kasch's claim is stronger than mere independence: projection and undercraft are negatively associated, so a performer's projection score is informative, just in the opposite direction most people expect. The 'one underlying quality' distractor is the halo instinct the whole section exists to correct -- an audience-commanding performer is not more likely to hold a scene together backstage; if anything, sustaining that level of projection narrows the attention undercraft requires. The uncorrelated version undersells the finding by removing the direction entirely, and the training-independence version misses that pushing projection actively competes for the same attentional resource undercraft draws on. (Undercraft Theory -> Two kinds of contribution)
takeaway: Projection and undercraft don't just fail to predict each other -- knowing one tells you something, in the opposite direction from what most readers expect.

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who retained the negative-association claim can identify what the summary understates before seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might notice the stem's claim sounds reasonable and pick the option that simply affirms it (the uncorrelated reading), which fails because the section's central finding is specifically that the relationship has a direction, not merely that it exists or doesn't.

stem: Troupe A's anchor performer needed exactly one backstage correction all night and made it invisibly; Troupe B's anchor performer needed thirty corrections and caught every single one invisibly. Both score a Fen index of 1.0. What does this pair of nights show about the Fen index and the correction load?

options.text: The Fen index is a rate, not a count -- it says nothing about how often correction was needed, so the matching score hides that Troupe B's performer carried a far heavier correction load.
Troupe A's performer must be the less skilled of the two, since catching thirty corrections cleanly all night is a harder demonstration of skill than catching just one.
options.provenance: misreads the claim that both score 1.0 as counterintuitive evidence the metric is broken, rather than the defining property of a rate

options.text: Since both performers scored an identical 1.0, their nights were equally smooth, with roughly the same number of things going wrong backstage for each of them.
options.provenance: misreads the success-rate definition as also telling you how often corrections were needed

options.text: The Fen index also counts corrections that could conceivably have arisen but never did, which is why Troupe B's larger set of possible problems still produced the same score.
options.provenance: misreads 'proportion of attempted corrections' as covering corrections that were never actually attempted

explanation: The Fen index measures success among attempted corrections, so a performer who needed one correction and made it, and one who needed thirty and made all thirty, score identically -- correction load is Kasch's separate, deliberately independent count of how much trouble a performer actually faced. The tempting answer that Troupe A's performer is 'less skilled' mistakes a smaller sample for a weaker one; a rate does not reward volume. Reading the matching score as evidence of an equally smooth night, or as covering corrections that never arose, both blur the same distinction: the Fen index and the correction load are two separate quantities, and a troupe can carry an excellent rate alongside a crushing load. (Undercraft Theory -> The Fen index)
takeaway: A Fen index tells you how reliably a performer corrects; only the correction load tells you how often they had to.

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who understood that the Fen index is a rate rather than a count could name the correction-load gap without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might reason that catching thirty corrections 'sounds more impressive' and pick the option ranking Troupe B's performer as more skilled, which fails because a rate is defined to be blind to volume by construction.

stem: A touring director is casting a new show. Performer X reliably draws the loudest audience reactions but has struggled in rehearsal to catch missed cues without being noticed. Performer Y draws little audience attention but has caught nearly every backstage problem cleanly and invisibly. Based on Kasch's casting findings, how should the director assign the lead and anchor positions?

options.text: X should be cast as the lead, the highest-projection-demand position, and Y as the anchor, the highest-correction-load, lowest-visibility position.
X should be cast as the anchor, since anchor is the show's most prominent and structurally important position, and X is clearly the stronger overall performer of the two.
options.provenance: misreads the anchor's structural centrality as visibility, conflating importance-to-the-show with importance-to-the-audience

options.text: X should be cast as the lead, and because leads carry the most responsibility for holding a scene together, X's struggles with missed cues are the most urgent problem to fix.
options.provenance: misreads high projection demand as implying high responsibility for undercraft, conflating the two axes the section separates

options.text: Y should be cast as the anchor, and because anchors absorb the correction load entirely, X as lead will need to do no backstage correction work at all.
options.provenance: misreads 'lowest correction load' as zero correction load rather than simply the least of it

explanation: Kasch's casting data runs opposite to intuition: the lead, the position audiences watch most, goes to the strongest projector and carries the lowest correction load, while the anchor -- named for its position in the sightline dead zone -- goes to the weakest projector and carries the highest correction load. Treating 'anchor' as a synonym for 'most important, therefore most prominent' is the halo fallacy applied to blocking. Assuming the lead is also responsible for the bulk of undercraft, or that the lead does none at all, both collapse two positions built to divide exactly opposite demands -- the lead does still some correction work, just the least in the show. (Undercraft Theory -> Casting the anchor)
takeaway: The role that looks most important to the audience is cast for the opposite reason from the role that is actually structurally load-bearing backstage.

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who holds the anchor/lead casting logic can assign X and Y correctly before the options are shown.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might default to 'the stronger performer gets the most important-sounding job' and cast X as anchor, which fails because the anchor is deliberately the least visible position, not the most prestigious one.

stem: A touring manager boasts: 'Our Fen index has been a flawless 1.0 for six months straight -- our undercraft has never been better.' Using Kasch's account of rescue, repair, and correction load, which objection has the most support?

options.text: A flawless Fen index built only from rescues, alongside a flat or growing correction load, is the diagnostic picture Kasch treats as most dangerous -- the troupe may have merely gotten skilled at surviving recurring problems, not repairing them.

There is no real objection to raise here: a flawless Fen index sustained for six months is, on its own, clear proof that backstage craft has genuinely gotten better, regardless of what the correction load happens to be doing.
options.provenance: misreads 'an excellent Fen index built entirely out of rescues and no repairs at all' as a mark of skill rather than checking the correction-load trend

options.text: The stronger objection is that a lower Fen index paired with a shrinking correction load would actually be the worse diagnostic picture, since the raw success rate has visibly declined over time.
options.provenance: misreads the comparison between the two troupe profiles backwards, reversing which one Kasch treats as the clearer warning sign

options.text: The best objection is that the manager is likely counting a run of especially effective rescues as repairs, since a repair is really just a rescue performed with enough confidence to look permanent.
options.provenance: misreads 'removes the underlying cause so the same correction never needs to be attempted again' as a better rescue rather than a categorically different, between-performance action

explanation: A perfect Fen index only tells you the troupe succeeds at whichever corrections it attempts; it says nothing about whether the same corrections keep coming back. Kasch's sharper warning is exactly this profile -- a heroic rate built from rescues alone, with a correction load that isn't shrinking -- because it means the troupe has gotten good at surviving its own unfixed mistakes rather than eliminating them. The reversal claiming a lower Fen index with a shrinking load is worse gets Kasch's comparison backwards: a shrinking load means repairs are actually working, even though the raw rate looks worse on paper. And a repair is not just a confident rescue; it is a between-performance fix aimed at making the correction unnecessary next time. (Undercraft Theory -> Rescue, repair, and the correction load)
takeaway: A perfect success rate on corrections you keep needing to make is a worse sign than a slightly lower rate on a shrinking pile of problems.

citation.subheading: Rescue, repair, and the correction load

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who holds the rescue/repair and correction-load distinction can identify the danger in the manager's claim without the options in front of them.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might assume 'flawless metric equals flawless outcome' and pick the no-objection option, which fails because the stem explicitly supplies the one variable, the correction load, that the manager's boast conveniently omits.

stem: Over a touring season, a troupe's audience-rated gloss score climbs steadily month after month. What can we responsibly conclude about the troupe's undercraft from this trend alone, per Kasch's account of the gloss effect?

options.text: Very little on its own -- gloss tracks projection reliably, but it can rise even as the Fen index falls, since a confident cover of a visible stumble often reads as tighter craft than it is.

The undercraft has clearly improved, since an audience rating a show as more seamless is responding to a real increase in how well backstage problems are caught, night after night, throughout the season.
options.provenance: misreads a confident, well-projected cover of a visible stumble as evidence of tight craft rather than of a successful cover

options.text: Gloss should track the Fen index just as reliably as it tracks projection quality, so a rising gloss score is solid evidence that the troupe's undercraft has kept pace as well.
options.provenance: misreads 'gloss rises reliably with a troupe's average projection quality' as extending to the Fen index, reversing the point that the two can move in opposite directions

options.text: Gloss and the Fen index are really two measurements of the same underlying quality of a show, so a rise in one is good evidence of a matching rise in the other across an entire touring season.
options.provenance: misreads an audience-report measure and a backstage-logged measure as interchangeable proxies for 'how good the troupe is'

explanation: Gloss is an audience-facing measure, so it moves with projection, not with backstage success -- Kasch found it can climb through a season even as the Fen index quietly falls, because a confident, well-projected recovery from a visible stumble often gets rated more seamless than a scene that needed no recovery at all. The tempting reading -- that rising acclaim means better undercraft -- mistakes the cover for the craft, exactly the gap this section exists to name. Gloss doesn't track the Fen index the way it tracks projection, and the two are measuring genuinely different things: what the audience notices versus what backstage logs record. (Undercraft Theory -> The gloss effect)
takeaway: Rising audience acclaim for a show's smoothness can be evidence of better cover, not better craft.

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who knows gloss tracks projection rather than the Fen index can state the 'very little' answer before seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper would assume rising audience approval must mean broad improvement and pick the 'clearly improved' option, which fails because the section's whole point is that this specific inference is unreliable.

stem: A veteran performer known for commanding entire houses with high-energy work turns out, in backstage logs, to have one of the lowest Fen indices in her troupe. A colleague concludes she must simply care less about the ensemble than her castmates do. Which explanation does Kasch's account of the halo fallacy actually support?

options.text: Sustaining projection at full scale narrows a performer's peripheral awareness of the rest of the stage, which leaves less attention free for backstage correction -- an attentional limit, not a difference in effort, care, or commitment to the ensemble.

She simply cares less about the ensemble than her castmates do, and her weak backstage record is exactly the evidence a director needs to see that this is true, regardless of what audiences think of her.
options.provenance: misreads the attentional explanation ('attentional, not moral') as a claim about effort or character rather than divided attention

options.text: Since she commands the audience's attention more completely than anyone else in the troupe, she is clearly the strongest overall performer and should also be the one most reliable backstage when something goes wrong.
options.provenance: misreads audience command of attention as implying backstage reliability -- the halo fallacy stated as the naive assumption the section overturns

options.text: Her low Fen index and her strong projection are simply unrelated facts about her as a performer, and their both showing up in the same person is nothing more than coincidence, unconnected to how either skill is trained.
options.provenance: misreads 'not two ends of one scale' as meaning the two axes are merely unrelated rather than pulling against each other, applied to a single performer's case

explanation: Kasch's explanation for the halo fallacy is attentional, not moral: sustaining projection at full scale takes up the peripheral awareness undercraft depends on, so a performer working hardest to be seen has the least attention left for what she isn't supposed to be seen doing. The 'she cares less' reading imports a character judgment the section explicitly rules out. The 'should be more reliable backstage' option is the halo fallacy stated plainly -- audience command doesn't transfer to backstage reliability, and Kasch's data runs the other way. Treating the pattern as coincidence ignores that this is a systematic, negative association, not a random co-occurrence in one performer. (Undercraft Theory -> The halo fallacy)
takeaway: Command of the room and reliability behind it draw on the same finite attention, which is why they trade off.

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who has the attentional mechanism can state it as the explanation before seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might reach for the 'she must care less' option since it sounds like a plausible real-world judgment, but the passage explicitly rules out a moral explanation in favor of an attentional one.

stem: Kasch found that average Fen index peaks for troupes of five to seven performers -- the core band -- and declines for troupes below four and troupes above ten. A director notices that both a three-person troupe and a fourteen-person troupe show unusually low Fen indices, and concludes both are suffering the identical problem: not enough attentive people to catch backstage issues. What is wrong with this explanation?

options.text: The two declines are mechanically different: the small troupe lacks redundancy to cover someone pulled into projection, while the large troupe has too many signaling pairs to stay coordinated even though enough people are available.

Nothing is wrong with it -- both troupes are simply short on attentive people, whether that shortage comes from having too few performers or from the demands of a fourteen-person show spreading everyone thin.
options.provenance: misreads the two size-based declines as one undifferentiated 'too big or too small' effect, collapsing redundancy scarcity and signaling-network overload into a single mechanism

options.text: Larger troupes should always show a higher Fen index than smaller ones, since more performers means more hands free to cover a problem, so the fourteen-person troupe's low score is most likely a measurement error.
options.provenance: misreads the two intuitive guesses in 'the intuitive guess runs in one of two directions' as the actual finding, missing that Kasch found neither monotonic pattern

options.text: Both troupes likely have low audience-rated gloss scores, and since gloss and the Fen index move together, their low ratings from audiences explain why their measured Fen indices are also low.
options.provenance: misapplies the gloss/Fen-index conflation from elsewhere in the section to a troupe-size case where gloss is never discussed

explanation: The two failure modes are mechanically distinct, not a shared 'too few attentive people' problem. Below four performers, a troupe lacks redundancy: pulling one person into full projection leaves no one free to cover the gap. Above ten, the problem isn't headcount but coordination -- undercraft depends on fast, often nonverbal signaling between whoever is free, and the number of possible signaling pairs grows fast enough that cues get missed even with plenty of hands available. The 'always higher with more performers' distractor is one of the two intuitive guesses Kasch's data actually rules out. And gloss, an audience-facing measure, has no established relationship to troupe size at all -- borrowing it here conflates two separate metrics from elsewhere in the framework. (Undercraft Theory -> Troupe size and the core band)
takeaway: A large troupe's undercraft problem is a coordination-network problem, not a headcount problem -- the opposite failure from a small troupe's.

citation.subheading: Troupe size and the core band

load_bearing_figures: the core band of five to seven performers, with decline below four and above ten

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who retained the two distinct mechanisms, redundancy scarcity and signaling overload, can state the flaw in the director's reasoning unaided.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might reach for 'medium-size groups are just easier to manage' as a generic heuristic and pick the option treating both declines as one thing, which fails because the section names two different mechanisms on either side of the band.

stem: A student summarizes the field's history this way: 'Ferrant showed that the projection/undercraft distinction itself doesn't hold up.' Which classification of Ferrant's actual objection is accurate?

options.text: Ferrant accepted the projection/undercraft distinction and objected only to how 'invisible' was measured -- she argued backstage observers were folding two different audience responses, true non-detection and noticed-but-forgiven, into a single category.

Ferrant rejected the distinction wholesale, arguing that undercraft is really just an unrecognized form of projection, and that backstage observers have simply been sorting one real skill into two invented categories.
options.provenance: misreads the presence of a 'chief critic' as a wholesale rejection, when the text states she did not dispute the projection-undercraft distinction and attacked only the measurement of invisibility

options.text: Ferrant showed that Kasch's original backstage-observer method already separated a truly unnoticed correction from one the audience noticed but forgave, and her real contribution was mainly statistical refinement.
options.provenance: misreads Kasch's original backstage-observer method as already distinguishing these, when Ferrant's point is that it classified both as one 'invisible' category

options.text: Ferrant's real objection was that projection, not undercraft, is what audiences are responding to when they rate a show's seamlessness, which is the same conflation the gloss effect describes.
options.provenance: misapplies the gloss-effect conflation from a different subsection to Ferrant's specific methodological point about measuring invisibility

explanation: Ferrant's target was narrower than a rejection of the framework: the passage is explicit that she "did not dispute the projection-undercraft distinction" and attacked only the measurement of invisibility, arguing that backstage observers were lumping a truly unnoticed correction together with one the audience noticed and simply forgave. The "rejected wholesale" option overreads "chief critic" as a wholesale takedown. The "already separated" option gets the history backwards -- Kasch's original method is exactly what Ferrant says failed to separate the two cases, which is why his revised exit-questionnaire protocol exists and remains unused at scale. Borrowing the gloss effect here misapplies a different conflation to Ferrant's specific methodological point. (Undercraft Theory -> Ferrant's objection)
takeaway: A challenge to how a distinction was measured is not the same as a challenge to the distinction itself.

self_check.cover_test: Yes -- a reader who recalls that Ferrant's target was the measurement of invisibility, not the distinction itself, can produce the key without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might assume any named 'critic' must be rejecting the theory outright and pick the wholesale-rejection option, which fails because the passage explicitly limits her challenge to measurement.

note: Covered 10 of the 12 earns_question ideas in 8 candidates by spanning both live discrimination_pairs entries: UT-4/UT-5 (candidate 02, Fen index rate vs. correction load count) and UT-7/UT-8 (candidate 03, anchor vs. lead casting) each get a single contrast candidate rather than two separate ones, per the shard-design note that this is usually the better answer. UT-2 and UT-9 were left unshipped: UT-2 (undercraft succeeds by vanishing) is real but its cleanest angle -- a noticed-but-charming recovery still counting as success -- overlaps heavily with the gloss-effect material already carried by candidate 05 and would read as a near-duplicate stem; UT-9 (rescue vs. repair, plain definition) is explicitly noted in the map as subordinate to UT-10, which ships instead as the stronger L5 diagnostic-reversal question. All five lenses are represented (misconception x2, contrast x2, objection x2, case x1, figure x1); stem_format is capped at 2 uses each (claim-evaluation x2, classification x2, two-scenario/mechanism/thought-experiment/direct-conceptual x1 each). Only one candidate (07) carries a load-bearing durable figure, respecting the section's R11 budget of one; the three volatile figures (-0.35 correlation, forty troupes, Ferrant's 1971 survey of twelve) were not used as load-bearing anywhere.
